content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Heaven' primarily signifies the dwelling place of God — the transcendent realm of God's presence, throne, and glory — and, derivatively, the eternal destiny or home of the redeemed, where believers experience unbroken fellowship with God. It stands symbolically for divine transcendence, holiness, and the consummated blessedness promised to the faithful.", "primary_basis": ["Genesis 1:1 (God creates the heavens and the earth)", "1 Kings 8:27, 30 (heaven as God's dwelling place, though it cannot contain him)", "Psalm 11:4; Psalm 103:19 (the LORD's throne is in heaven)", "Isaiah 66:1 (heaven is my throne, the earth my footstool)", "Matthew 6:9 (Our Father who art in heaven)", "Matthew 5:12; 6:19-20 (reward and treasure laid up in heaven)", "John 14:2-3 (in my Father's house are many rooms; I go to prepare a place for you)", "2 Corinthians 5:1 (a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens)", "Philippians 3:20 (our citizenship is in heaven)", "Colossians 3:1-2 (set your minds on things above)", "Hebrews 9:24 (Christ entered heaven itself, now to appear in God's presence)", "1 Peter 1:4 (an inheritance kept in heaven)", "Revelation 4:1-11 (the heavenly throne room)", "Revelation 21:1-4; 22:1-5 (new heaven and new earth; God dwelling with his people)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Physical/cosmological sense: 'heaven(s)' as the sky, firmament, and celestial bodies — part of created order rather than a symbolic-theological realm (the 'first heaven' in traditional tripartite readings drawing on 2 Corinthians 12:2).", "basis": ["Genesis 1:6-8, 14-17", "Psalm 19:1", "Deuteronomy 10:14", "2 Corinthians 12:2 (third heaven implies lower heavens)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "'Kingdom of heaven' as a reverential circumlocution for God's reign or kingship (Matthew's substitution for 'kingdom of God'), so 'heaven' functions as a metonym for God himself rather than a place.", "basis": ["Matthew 3:2; 4:17; 13 (kingdom of heaven parables)", "Luke 15:18 (I have sinned against heaven)", "Daniel 4:26 (Heaven rules)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Heaven not as the final destination but as God's dimension that will ultimately be joined with a renewed earth — the 'new heavens and new earth' emphasis (prominent in recent biblical theology, e.g., N. T. Wright), which treats disembodied 'going to heaven' as at most an intermediate state.", "basis": ["Isaiah 65:17; 66:22", "Romans 8:19-23", "2 Peter 3:13", "Revelation 21:1-3 (the New Jerusalem descends to earth)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Heaven as a state or condition of perfect communion with God rather than a spatial location — the beatific vision emphasis in Catholic and classical theology (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1023-1029 describes heaven as the state of supreme, definitive happiness in seeing God).", "basis": ["1 Corinthians 13:12 (then face to face)", "1 John 3:2 (we shall see him as he is)", "Matthew 5:8 (the pure in heart shall see God)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Purely metaphorical, psychological, or existential readings: heaven as a symbol of inner spiritual state, moral ideal, or human hope rather than an objective postmortem reality (found in liberal Protestant, process, and some modern critical interpretation).", "basis": ["Luke 17:21 ('the kingdom of God is within/among you,' extended by analogy)", "General demythologizing hermeneutics (e.g., Bultmann) rather than specific proof texts"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "'Heavenly places' as a present spiritual sphere of authority and conflict that believers already inhabit in Christ (Pauline usage in Ephesians), distinct from heaven as future destiny.", "basis": ["Ephesians 1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12"], "prominence": "common"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that heaven denotes God's dwelling/presence and the eternal blessedness of the redeemed. The live disputes concern mode rather than core meaning: place vs. state, present spiritual reality vs. future destination, disembodied intermediate state vs. embodied life on a renewed earth, and how much of the biblical language is ancient cosmology versus theological symbol. The Hebrew 'shamayim' and Greek 'ouranos' both cover 'sky' and 'God's realm,' which drives much of the interpretive variation."}
